AIBAST Agents Library

Why the RAPP Brainstem?

It is a local frontier learning and rapid prototyping tool. It is where you learn the agent pattern and prove a prototype on your own machine, before the result graduates into the Microsoft tools that carry it to real users.

What it is

A private practice space where you describe real work in ordinary language and watch GitHub Copilot turn it into a working AI skill. You see the files appear, watch the skill run, review the result, and ask Copilot to improve anything that does not work.

There is no cloud environment to prepare before learning begins. The library's industry solutions and Academy workshops give you realistic starting points, synthetic examples, and visible tests so you can learn by doing rather than by sitting through another presentation.

What it is not

  • Not a replacement for GitHub Copilot. Copilot is the work surface and the model. The Brainstem borrows Copilot's access so there are no keys to manage, and it hands the work back to Copilot the moment you are done learning.
  • Not a competitor to Copilot Studio or Microsoft 365 Copilot. Those are where a finished agent lives. The Brainstem is where the agent is first understood, and the library ships the Copilot Studio solution for every workshop precisely so the prototype can leave.
  • Not a production runtime. Nothing here is built to serve users. It is built to teach one person at a time, quickly.
  • Not another platform to learn. The learner talks to Copilot, watches the work happen, and leaves with a reusable skill. The technical plumbing stays in the background.

Why local, and why "frontier"

The fastest way to learn is to try something, watch it work, change it, and try again. Doing that in a production tenant introduces permissions, publishing, and real-user risk before the learner understands the pattern. Doing it locally keeps the first experiment small, visible, and easy to reset.

Frontier means this is where new AI capabilities are explored first. The supplied workshops use synthetic data and stop before real-world actions. Useful patterns graduate into reviewed solutions. Unhelpful experiments can be discarded without disrupting anyone.

Why it works with the tools people already use

Teams already work across SharePoint, Dynamics, Microsoft 365, local files, and conversations. RAPP does not ask everyone to abandon those tools for one new application. It helps turn a useful way of working into a portable skill that can meet people where they already are.

  • Keep information where it belongs. Learning a workflow does not require copying every source into a new system.
  • Meet people where they work. A proven skill can later appear through Copilot Studio, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Teams, or another experience that fits the user.
  • Give each role the right view. A seller, architect, operator, and leader can use the same underlying capability without needing the same screen or level of detail.
  • Use the AI assistant that fits the moment. Copilot can build the skill, another supported assistant can help inspect or improve it, and the learner keeps the result.

The screen, model, and destination may change. The useful part—the learned workflow and proof that it works—can stay with the person and the team.

Local does not mean isolated

Local-first protects the earliest learning loop: private context stays close to the learner, experiments are inexpensive, and unfinished work is not automatically published. Once something works, the learner can share the skill and its evidence without sharing an entire chat history or private workspace.

  • Personalize locally. Adapt a workspace or agent to a role, account, or workflow without forcing everyone into the same interface.
  • Share deliberately. Share the reviewed skill and safe evidence instead of copying private data or every conversation that produced it.
  • Improve together. A useful local improvement can strengthen the shared version while each person keeps the version that fits their work.

The useful "hive" is not one giant pool of everyone's raw information. It is a team learning from portable capabilities that people intentionally choose to share.

What the learner actually does

  1. Describe the work. Start with a real outcome in ordinary language.
  2. Watch Copilot build it. The files, tools, and decisions remain visible instead of disappearing behind a demo.
  3. Run it immediately. Use synthetic examples to see what the skill does and where it fails.
  4. Improve it through conversation. Correct the result, rerun the test, and watch the capability get better.
  5. Keep the skill. The useful learning becomes a reusable file, not a good answer trapped in yesterday's chat.

Why the learning sticks

A prompt can produce a helpful answer once. RAPP turns the lesson behind that answer into something the learner can see, run, test, change, and reuse. The learner does not have to trust a slide or a polished demonstration—they watch the real workflow complete.

The permanent result is not the conversation. It is the small skill, the decisions that shaped it, and the evidence that it worked. A fresh conversation can pick up that useful context without carrying every stale instruction and detour from the chats that came before.

The graduation path

StageWhereWhat you have at the end
LearnThe Brainstem on your machineA working single-file agent you understand line by line
ProveAcademy workshops and the production guideLocked test cases passing, evidence captured, a reviewed draft
ShipGitHub Copilot, Copilot Studio, Microsoft 365 CopilotThe same learned workflow, adapted for the place your users already work

The library calls these the Brainstem, the Hippocampus, and the Nervous System. The names are a mnemonic for the same idea: start with the survival loop, add memory and a cloud body when you need them, then connect to the enterprise nervous system. You advance when you choose to.

How it stays out of the way

  • No separate model key. The Brainstem uses your existing GitHub Copilot access instead of asking you to create and manage another model-provider credential.
  • Your work is visible. The skill and its local memory are files you can inspect, back up, keep, or delete.
  • Skills stay small. One portable agent file is easier to understand, review, share, and improve.
  • Copilot does the technical work. The learner can stay in conversation while Copilot handles files, tests, and setup in view.
  • You can leave cleanly. The useful learning stays in the skill file rather than being trapped inside the Brainstem.

How it compares

Several projects share one piece of this idea. None combines all four: your existing GitHub Copilot as the model, a skill that is a small program you can read and run, a library of industry starting points with sample data, and a path into Copilot Studio and Microsoft 365.

If you wantThe closest alternativeWhat the Brainstem adds
An assistant with add-onsOpenClaw and its ClawHub registryIts skills are mostly written instructions the model follows. A Brainstem skill is a program that gives the same answer every run, and it graduates into Microsoft 365.
Agents in a folder, behind a chatDatabricks AppKit agents pluginThat plugin reads its agents folder when the app starts, inside a Databricks workspace. The Brainstem runs on a laptop and picks up a new skill on the next message.
A shared directory of agentsAGNTCY (OASF records and the Agent Directory Service)It lists descriptions of agents. The library ships the agent itself, with sample data, tests and a Copilot Studio solution.
An agent you can save and moveLetta Agent FileA Letta agent moves between Letta servers. A Brainstem skill is one file that runs in any Brainstem and graduates to Copilot Studio.
A place to share skillsskills.sh and Docker AgentThose share instruction folders and configuration files. The library shares working agents with a path into the tools your users already have.
Details and sources
  • OpenClaw and ClawHub. OpenClaw runs its own agent runtime. ClawHub is its public registry for skills and plugins, with one-command install, versions and ranking by stars and downloads. Skills are versioned SKILL.md text bundles. ClawHub docs
  • Databricks AppKit agents plugin (beta). It scans server/agents/<id>/ at startup, and the folder name becomes the agent id. It serves a streaming POST /chat and a single-response POST /invocations, and keeps conversation threads on the server. Plugin docs
  • AGNTCY. Agent records are addressed by their SHA-256 digest, packaged as OCI artifacts, optionally signed with Sigstore, and described with a shared skill vocabulary. The directory describes agents rather than running them, and it is an individual IETF draft. Paper · Draft
  • Letta Agent File (.af). One file holds an agent's memory, tool code, system prompt, message history and model settings, with secrets removed on export. It is tied to the Letta runtime. Agent File docs
  • skills.sh and Docker Agent. npx skills add installs SKILL.md folders into many agent hosts, and skills.sh ranks them by installs. Docker Agent shares a YAML agent through any OCI registry. skills · Docker Agent

Compiled October 2026 from each project's own documentation. These projects change quickly, so check the linked pages for current details.

Ten prompts that show the difference

Ten small things to try, in order. Together they turn one chore into a tool your team can use. Nothing here needs you to write code. Prompts 1, 4 and 8 go to GitHub Copilot. The others go to the Brainstem chat.

Ten prompts, in order, that take one idea from a sentence to a skill your team uses. Each one shows something you would otherwise have to fake or hand-build. Prompts 1, 4 and 8 go to GitHub Copilot. The others go to the Brainstem chat.

Ten prompts that exercise the parts no single alternative above combines: deterministic single-file tools, hot reload, inspectable tool output, file-based memory and a promotion path into Microsoft 365. Prompts 1, 4 and 8 go to GitHub Copilot. The others go to the Brainstem chat.

  1. Turn your routine into a skill GitHub Copilot
    In the Brainstem agents folder, write a skill named weekly_revenue_drop_agent.py. It takes last week's and this week's revenue per account as text like "Contoso 120000, Fabrikam 80000", works out the change for each account, and lists the accounts that dropped, largest percent drop first.

    What you see: a new file appears in the agents folder, small enough to read in a minute.

    Why it matters to you: Something you do by hand every week becomes a button you can press. You describe it in plain words; Copilot builds it.

    Why it matters to you: You describe the chore once and get a real tool, not a prompt you paste and hope about every Monday.

    Why it matters to you: The output is a deterministic Python tool (a BasicAgent with metadata and perform), not a SKILL.md the model reinterprets on every call.

    Why elsewhere falls short: instruction-based skills ask the model to redo the arithmetic every time; this one calculates.

  2. Use it immediately Brainstem
    Use the weekly revenue drop skill on these numbers and show me exactly what you sent it and what it returned. Last week: Contoso 118000, Fabrikam 64000, Northwind 47000. This week: Contoso 99000, Fabrikam 66000, Northwind 30000.

    What you see: Northwind down 36 percent, Contoso down 16 percent, Fabrikam left out because it grew, with the exact inputs and outputs.

    Why it matters to you: It works the moment it exists. Nothing to install, restart or publish.

    Why it matters to you: No deploy loop: save, ask, see. You iterate as fast as you can type a message.

    Why it matters to you: agents/*_agent.py is rediscovered on every /chat request, so a new file is live on the next call with no server restart.

    Why elsewhere falls short: folder-based servers such as the Databricks plugin load agents when the app starts.

  3. Catch a skill that only pretends Brainstem
    Run the weekly revenue drop skill on Last week: Contoso 118000, Northwind 47000. This week: Contoso 99000, Northwind 30000. Then tell me: did the skill do the math, or did you? Quote its reply word for word.

    What you see: the skill's reply quoted exactly, plus a check of its figures. If a skill only repeats its input, the answer says so plainly.

    Why it matters to you: You can tell whether the computer actually worked something out, or just sounded sure of itself.

    Why it matters to you: It catches the classic AI failure, a tool that looks finished but only echoes, before your users do.

    Why it matters to you: Every /chat response carries agent_logs with the raw tool output, so you can tell tool results from model text without a tracing stack.

    Why elsewhere falls short: most hosts need a separate tracing service to show this. Here the record comes back with every answer, on your own machine.

  4. Change it by asking GitHub Copilot
    Change the weekly revenue drop skill so it also lists any account that grew more than 25 percent, under its own heading. Keep everything else the same.

    What you see: a small, readable change to one file. Ask the Brainstem prompt 2 again and the new section appears.

    Why it matters to you: Want it a little different? Say so in one sentence, and it changes.

    Why it matters to you: Change requests are one sentence, and the change is small enough to eyeball.

    Why it matters to you: Edits land as a small diff to one file that the next request picks up. Review is a git diff, not a platform redeploy.

    Why elsewhere falls short: a change to an agent built on a hosted platform usually means a redeploy.

  5. Start from your industry Brainstem
    Using the action prioritization agent and its sample pipeline, what are the three things this rep should do first today, and why?

    What you see: a day plan for a sample sales rep, built from the agent's own synthetic data, with the reasoning behind the order.

    Why it matters to you: Start from an example made for your kind of work, with pretend data, so nothing private is at risk.

    Why it matters to you: Skip the blank page: take a working industry agent and bend it to your case.

    Why it matters to you: Templates ship as runnable agents with built-in synthetic data, not just catalog metadata.

    Why elsewhere falls short: agent directories such as AGNTCY describe agents; the library ships one you can run.

  6. Memory you can open Brainstem
    Remember this for later: our fiscal year starts on July 1.

    Then, in a new conversation: Which fiscal quarter does next March fall in for us?

    What you see: “fiscal Q3” in a conversation that never heard the fact. The fact sits in a plain file next to the Brainstem.

    Why it matters to you: It remembers what you tell it, and you can open that memory like a document, or delete it.

    Why it matters to you: Your project facts follow you from chat to chat, with no database to set up.

    Why it matters to you: Memory persists to .brainstem_data/shared_memories/memory.json: readable, diffable and portable, with no server database.

    Why elsewhere falls short: server-based agents such as Letta keep memory in the server's database.

  7. Teach it back Brainstem
    Explain to me, in plain words, what the weekly revenue drop skill does, what it needs from me, and when I should not trust its answer.

    What you see: a plain explanation, including the cases where the skill's answer would mislead you.

    Why it matters to you: You understand what you made well enough to explain it to a coworker the same day.

    Why it matters to you: You learn what you shipped, including how it can fail, without reading the code.

    Why it matters to you: The skill's metadata (description and parameters) is its documentation, and the model explains it from the same schema it calls.

    Why elsewhere falls short: an agent spread across server settings, prompts and plugins is hard to explain in one sitting.

  8. Hand it to a teammate GitHub Copilot
    Write a short note for a teammate explaining how to drop weekly_revenue_drop_agent.py into their Brainstem's agents folder and which question to ask first.

    What you see: a three-step note. The teammate copies one file and asks prompt 2 on their own machine.

    Why it matters to you: Sharing is like sending an attachment. Your teammate gets the tool, not your private chats.

    Why it matters to you: Sharing is one file: no account, no export flow, no workspace invite.

    Why it matters to you: A single-file agent is the whole unit of sharing, with no export or import tied to one runtime.

    Why elsewhere falls short: a Letta agent moves by export and import between Letta servers.

  9. Graduate it Copilot Studio · needs a Microsoft 365 tenant
    Which Academy workshop is closest to the weekly revenue drop skill, and walk me through importing its Copilot Studio solution so my team can use it in Teams.

    What you see: the matching workshop and its ready-made Copilot Studio solution, then import steps.

    Why it matters to you: When it is good, your whole team can use it inside Teams, where they already work.

    Why it matters to you: Your prototype has a real path to the people who will use it, instead of dying on your laptop.

    Why it matters to you: Promotion path: local Brainstem, then the Azure Functions tier, then a Copilot Studio solution, with the same skill contract.

    Why elsewhere falls short: none of the alternatives above has a path into Copilot Studio or Microsoft 365.

  10. Get unstuck, keep control Frontier beta
    I'm stuck. Take over this chat, finish the skill, then give me back control and tell me what you changed.

    What you see: another AI drives the same visible chat you were using, finishes the work, and hands it back with a summary.

    Why it matters to you: If you get stuck, an assistant finishes the job while you watch, then hands the controls back.

    Why it matters to you: Never stuck for long: hand over the wheel, watch it drive, take it back.

    Why it matters to you: Frontier beta: an outside agent drives the visible chat (not a hidden background job), then returns control.

    What is different: the help happens in the learner's own chat, in view, rather than in a hidden background job.

Prompts 1 to 7 were checked on a fresh local Brainstem in October 2026. Prompt 9 needs a Microsoft 365 tenant, and prompt 10 needs the Frontier beta.

Who it is for

Sellers, architects, and partners who need to understand an agent pattern well enough to explain it and adapt it, and workshop learners who want to build one before they publish one. If you already know what you want to ship, go straight to the library and take the Copilot Studio solution. If you want to understand it first, install the Brainstem.
